name: Angola
snapshot: An oil state still governed by the MPLA, the movement that won the 1975 to 2002 civil war, with a young, fast-growing and increasingly restless population.
culture: Angola's culture mixes Portuguese colonial heritage with Kimbundu, Ovimbundu and Bakongo traditions. Luanda is the home of semba, the ancestor of Brazilian samba, and of kuduro, a frenetic dance music born in the 1990s musseques, the informal neighbourhoods. Kizomba, a slow partner dance, has spread from Angola across the Portuguese-speaking world. Portuguese is the official language and the first language of a growing urban majority.
society: Oil makes up most exports, but wealth has been concentrated in a small elite; the daughter of former president José Eduardo dos Santos was once Africa's richest woman. Around half the population is under 16. Many Luandans live in informal settlements without reliable water. The US-backed Lobito rail corridor to the Congo and Zambia copper belt is the government's big bet on diversification.
situation: João Lourenço, president since 2017, won a second term in 2022 in the closest election in Angola's history, with the opposition UNITA taking the capital. Fuel subsidy cuts in July 2025 set off deadly protests and riots in Luanda. With Lourenço barred from running again in 2027, 2026 has been dominated by the MPLA's succession question: the president has dropped hints without naming an heir, and critics accuse the courts of sidelining would-be rivals. The US- backed Lobito rail corridor to the Congo and Zambia copper belt is his flagship project.
power: A presidential republic in which the head of the winning party list in the National Assembly election becomes president, for at most two five-year terms. The president heads the government. The MPLA has ruled since independence in 1975.
